Branching Strategy - Introduction

We use trunk-based development. `main` is always releasable, and all work is
merged into it through short-lived branches.

chunk_body:
| Branch | Created from | Merges into | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| `main` | n/a | n/a | The trunk. Protected; no direct pushes. |
| `feature/<ticket-id>-<summary>` | `main` | `main` | New work and fixes. |
| `hotfix/<ticket-id>` | release tag | release, then `main` | Urgent production fixes. |
| `release/<version>` | `main` | none | Only for services that ship on a fixed schedule. |

Using the Build Server - Introduction

All product builds run on the Jenkins build server, `build01.corp.local`,
which sits in the server room on the 4th floor. This guide explains how to
set up a job for your project, trigger a build and pick up the result.

chunk_body:
Ask the Build and Release team for a Jenkins account through a HelpLine
ticket under *Access*. Your account uses your Windows username; you set a
separate Jenkins password the first time you log in at
`http://build01.corp.local:8080`.
chunk_text:
Using the Build Server - Getting an account

Ask the Build and Release team for a Jenkins account through a HelpLine
ticket under *Access*. Your account uses your Windows username; you set a
separate Jenkins password the first time you log in at
`http://build01.corp.local:8080`.

chunk_body:
1. Copy the *template-maven* job and name the copy after your repository.
2. Under *Source Code Management*, enter the SVN URL of your project's
   trunk, for example `svn://svn.corp.local/repos/payments/trunk`.
3. Under *Build Triggers*, tick *Poll SCM* and keep the default schedule.
   Jenkins checks SVN for new commits and starts a build when it finds one.
4. Under *Post-build Actions*, add *Archive the artifacts* with
   `target/*.war`.
5. Click *Save*.

4. Under *Post-build Actions*, add *Archive the artifacts* with

chunk_body:
Answers to common questions about the continuous integration (CI) pipeline
that runs on every pull request.

**What does the pipeline run?**
Four stages, in order: lint, unit tests, build, and integration tests. The
build stage produces a container image that is pushed to the internal
registry. A stage only starts if the one before it passed.

**Why did my pipeline not start?**
Pipelines start when you push to a branch that has an open pull request. Draft
pull requests run lint and unit tests only. If nothing starts, check that the
repository has a `.ci.yml` file on your branch.

**A test failed but passes on my laptop. What now?**
First re-run the failed job once from the pull request page. If it passes on
re-run, the test is probably flaky: report it in #ci-help with a link to the
failed run so the owning team can fix it. Do not keep re-running until it
goes green.

**How do I see the logs?**
Click the failed check on the pull request, then **Details**. Logs are kept
for 90 days.

**Can I skip CI for a small change?**
No. Documentation-only changes run a shorter pipeline automatically, based on
the paths changed, but no change can skip CI entirely.

**Why is my pipeline queued?**
Runners are shared across all teams. Queues are longest in the late IST
afternoon. If a job has been queued for an unusually long time, post in
#ci-help.

**How do I add a secret to the pipeline?**
Never commit secrets to the repository. Ask your team lead to add the secret
in the CI settings for your repository. It is then available to jobs as an
environment variable.

**Who owns the pipeline?**
The Developer Experience team owns the shared pipeline templates. Your team
owns the `.ci.yml` file in its own repositories.

Code Review Process - Introduction

Every change to a shared repository goes through a pull request (PR) and at
least one review before it is merged. This page covers what authors and
reviewers are expected to do.

chunk_body:

  series of PRs that can each be reviewed on their own.
- Make sure the CI pipeline passes on your branch.
- Write a description that says what changed, why, and how you tested it.
  Link the ticket.
- Mark the PR as a draft if you want early feedback but it is not ready to
  merge.

chunk_body:
The Code Review Process sets out the rules every pull request must follow.
This guide goes further and explains how to review well. It is written for
engineers who have recently started reviewing, but experienced reviewers
may find it a useful reminder.
chunk_text:
Code Review Guide for Reviewers - Introduction

The Code Review Process sets out the rules every pull request must follow.
This guide goes further and explains how to review well. It is written for
engineers who have recently started reviewing, but experienced reviewers
may find it a useful reminder.

chunk_body:
Code review has three goals, in this order:

1. **Catch problems** before they reach production: bugs, security issues,
   missing tests and changes that will be hard to operate.
2. **Share knowledge** so that more than one person understands each part of
   the system.
3. **Keep the codebase consistent** so it stays easy to read and change.

Review is not a gate to show that you are more senior than the author, and
it is not a place to redesign a feature that has already been agreed.
chunk_text:
Code Review Guide for Reviewers - Why we review

1. **Catch problems** before they reach production: bugs, security issues,
   missing tests and changes that will be hard to operate.
2. **Share knowledge** so that more than one person understands each part of
   the system.
3. **Keep the codebase consistent** so it stays easy to read and change.

Review is not a gate to show that you are more senior than the author, and
it is not a place to redesign a feature that has already been agreed.

chunk_body:
- Read the pull request description and the linked ticket first. You cannot
  judge a change without knowing what it is meant to do.
- Check that CI has passed. If it has not, you can usually wait until it
  does before reviewing in detail.
- If the change is too large to review properly, say so politely and ask
  the author to split it. A review that skims a very large change catches
  little.
chunk_text:
Code Review Guide for Reviewers - Before you start

- Read the pull request description and the linked ticket first. You cannot
  judge a change without knowing what it is meant to do.
- Check that CI has passed. If it has not, you can usually wait until it
  does before reviewing in detail.
- If the change is too large to review properly, say so politely and ask
  the author to split it. A review that skims a very large change catches

chunk_body:
Work from the most important questions to the least important.

**Does it do the right thing?**
Does the change solve the problem in the ticket? Are there cases the author
has not handled, such as empty input, errors from other services, retries or
concurrent requests?

**Is it safe?**
Look for user input that reaches a database query or a shell command
unchecked, secrets in code or logs, personal data written to logs, and
permission checks that are missing. When in doubt, ask the security team to
review.

**Is it tested?**
New behaviour needs tests. Bug fixes need a test that fails without the fix.
Read the tests as carefully as the code: a test that cannot fail is worse
than no test.

**Can we run it?**
Will the on-call engineer understand what went wrong from the logs and
metrics? Does the change need a feature flag, a migration or an update to a
runbook? Is it backwards compatible with the version currently running?

**Is it clear?**
Are names clear? Is there a simpler way to write it? Would a short comment
help the next reader understand *why* the code is written this way?

**Does it follow our conventions?**
Formatting and most style rules are checked by linters in CI, so do not
spend review time on them. Comment only on conventions that tools cannot
check.

chunk_body:
- Be specific. "This loop will run once per user, so it makes one database
  call per user" is more useful than "this looks slow".
- Explain why. If you ask for a change, say what problem it solves.
- Ask questions when you are not sure. "What happens if this list is empty?"
  invites the author to explain, and you may learn something.
- Mark the weight of each comment. Use `nit:` for minor suggestions the
  author may ignore, and say clearly when something must change before
  merge.
- Praise good work. Pointing out a well-written test or a clear abstraction
  is part of sharing knowledge too.
- Keep the tone neutral. Written comments read more harshly than spoken
  ones. Write "we" and "this code", not "you".

- **Approve** when the change is ready to merge, even if you left a few
  nits. Trust the author to deal with them.
- **Comment** when you have questions but have not finished reviewing, or
  when you are not a code owner.
- **Request changes** only for problems that must be fixed before merge. When
  the author has addressed them, review again promptly and approve.

If you and the author cannot agree after a couple of exchanges, move the
discussion to a call or to your team channel. If you still disagree, ask
your tech lead to decide. Record the decision in the pull request so others
can see it later. Disagreements about style that no written convention
covers should usually go the author's way.

chunk_text:
Production Deployment Runbook - Introduction

This runbook describes how to deploy a service to production using the
shared deployment pipeline. It applies to every service that runs on the
company Kubernetes platform. Services with their own runbook may add steps,
but should not skip any of the checks below.

chunk_body:
Any engineer who is a member of the service's owning team in GitHub can
start a deployment. New engineers should do their first production
deployment with their onboarding buddy watching. Deployments of shared
platform components (ingress, service mesh, logging) can only be started by
the Platform team.

start a deployment. New engineers should do their first production
deployment with their onboarding buddy watching. Deployments of shared
platform components (ingress, service mesh, logging) can only be started by
the Platform team.

chunk_body:
- Deploy during working hours, Monday to Thursday, when the owning team is
  online to watch the release.
- Avoid deploying on Fridays, on the day before a public holiday, or during
  a declared change freeze. Change freezes are announced in
  #eng-announcements.
- Do not deploy while there is an open SEV1 or SEV2 incident affecting your
  service or its dependencies, unless the deployment is the fix.

chunk_body:
1. Check that the change is merged into `main` and that the CI pipeline for
   that commit passed.
2. Check that the change has been running in staging and that the staging
   dashboards look normal: error rate, latency and saturation.
3. If the change includes a database migration, confirm that it is backwards
   compatible. The old version of the service must keep working after the
   migration has run, because it will still be serving traffic during the
   rollout.
4. If the change is risky, put it behind a feature flag so you can turn it
   off without a rollback.
5. Post in your team channel that you are about to deploy, with a link to
   the pull request.

chunk_body:
1. Open the deployment pipeline for your service and choose the commit from
   `main` that you want to release.
2. Select **Deploy to production**. The pipeline tags the commit with the
   next version number and builds the release notes from the merged pull
   requests.
3. The pipeline runs any database migrations first, as a separate job. If
   the migration job fails, the deployment stops and nothing else changes.

2. Select **Deploy to production**. The pipeline tags the commit with the

3. The pipeline runs any database migrations first, as a separate job. If

chunk_body:
The new version is first sent a small share of production traffic. During
this stage:

- Watch the canary dashboard for your service. It compares the canary with
  the stable version side by side.
- The pipeline checks error rate and latency automatically. If either is
  clearly worse than the stable version, the pipeline stops the rollout and
  sends traffic back to the stable version.
- Look at the logs for new errors or warnings, even if the automatic checks
  pass. Automatic checks do not catch every problem.

If you are unsure whether the canary is healthy, do not promote it. Ask in
#platform-help or roll back.

- Look at the logs for new errors or warnings, even if the automatic checks

If you are unsure whether the canary is healthy, do not promote it. Ask in

chunk_body:
When you are satisfied with the canary, select **Promote**. The pipeline
moves the rest of the traffic to the new version in steps and waits between
each step. You can pause the rollout at any point.

After the rollout finishes:

- Keep watching the service dashboards and alerts for a while before you
  move on to other work.
- Check any user journeys the change affects, for example by using the
  feature yourself in production if it is safe to do so.
- Post in your team channel that the deployment is complete, with the new
  version number.

- If the problem is contained to a feature behind a flag, turning the flag
  off is usually faster than a rollback.
- If you roll back, or if the problem affected users, open an incident in
  #incidents so the response is tracked and a postmortem can be written if
  needed.

Short definitions of terms you will hear in engineering meetings, tickets and
runbooks.

**Blameless postmortem.** A written review after an incident that looks at
what happened and how to prevent it, without blaming individuals.

**Canary release.** Sending a new version to a small share of traffic first,
and widening it only if error rates stay normal.

**CODEOWNERS.** A file in each repository that lists which team owns which
paths. It decides who is asked to review a pull request.

**Feature flag.** A setting that turns a piece of code on or off without a new
deployment.

**Flaky test.** A test that sometimes passes and sometimes fails on the same
code.

**Incident commander.** The person who coordinates the response to a major
incident. It is usually the on-call primary until someone else takes over.

**Pull request (PR).** A request to merge changes from a branch into another
branch, where the changes are reviewed.

**Rollback.** Returning a service to its previous working version.

**Runbook.** Step-by-step instructions for operating a service or handling a
known problem.

**SLO (service level objective).** A target for how reliable a service should
be, such as the share of requests that succeed.

**Staging.** An environment that mirrors production, used for final checks
before a release.

**Trunk.** The main branch (`main`) that all work merges into.

Use a hotfix branch only for an urgent fix to what is running in production.

1. Branch from the latest release tag, not from `main`:
   `git switch -c hotfix/<ticket-id> v<release>`.
2. Make the smallest change that fixes the problem, with a test.
3. Open a pull request against the release tag's branch and label it
   `hotfix`. One approving review is enough.
4. After it is deployed, open a second pull request to bring the same fix
   into `main`.

Do not mix refactoring or unrelated changes into a hotfix.

**Classification: Restricted. Engineering only. Contains secret store paths
and approval rules.**

This runbook covers scheduled and emergency rotation of production
encryption keys and service secrets. All production secrets live in the
central secrets store under the path `kv/prod/<service>/<secret-name>`.
Nobody may keep a production secret anywhere else, including in CI
variables, except the short-lived tokens that the store issues itself.

chunk_body:
| Secret type | Rotation interval | How |
|---|---|---|
| Cloud KMS customer-managed keys | Every 365 days | Automatic; old key versions kept for decryption |
| Database service-account credentials | Every 90 days | Scheduled job `rotate-db-creds`, dual-running for 24 hours |
| Third-party API keys | Every 180 days | Manual, by the owning team |
| Internal service-to-service tokens | Every 7 hours | Automatic, issued by the secrets store |
| TLS certificates | 90-day certificates renewed automatically 20 days before expiry | ACME client |
| SSH certificate authority signing key | Every 2 years | Manual, Platform only |
| Payment gateway signing keys | Every 12 months, in the first week of March | Manual, with the gateway provider |

The Platform team publishes the rotation calendar in the #platform-rotations
channel each month.

chunk_body:
If users are affected and you suspect the latest deployment, roll back

chunk_text:
Production Rollback Runbook - The golden rule

If users are affected and you suspect the latest deployment, roll back
first and investigate afterwards. A rollback is a normal, safe operation.
Nobody will ask why you rolled back; they may ask why you did not.

chunk_body:
Roll back when:

- Error rates or latency got worse soon after the deployment.
- A feature changed in the deployment is broken for users.
- The canary checks passed but you see new errors in the logs that were not
  there before.

Consider other options first when:

- The broken code is behind a feature flag. Turning the flag off is faster
  and keeps the rest of the release.
- The problem is in a dependency, not in your service. Rolling back your
  service will not help; escalate to the owning team instead.
- The deployment included a database migration that is not backwards
  compatible. See the section on migrations below before you do anything.

Roll back when:

- Error rates or latency got worse soon after the deployment.
- A feature changed in the deployment is broken for users.
- The canary checks passed but you see new errors in the logs that were not
  there before.

Consider other options first when:

- The broken code is behind a feature flag. Turning the flag off is faster
  and keeps the rest of the release.
- The problem is in a dependency, not in your service. Rolling back your
  service will not help; escalate to the owning team instead.
- The deployment included a database migration that is not backwards
  compatible. See the section on migrations below before you do anything.

2. Open the **History** tab and find the last release that was healthy. This
   is usually the one immediately before the current release.
3. Select **Redeploy** on that release. The pipeline skips the canary stage
   for a rollback and moves traffic to the previous version in one step.
4. Watch the service dashboards until error rate and latency return to
   normal.
5. Post in your team channel and in the incident channel, if there is one,
   that you have rolled back and to which version.

The pipeline does not run database migrations in reverse during a rollback.
It only changes which version of the service code is running.

chunk_body:
Our migration rules require every migration to be backwards compatible, so
the previous version of the service can run against the migrated database.
If that rule was followed, a normal rollback is safe.

If you think a migration was not backwards compatible:

1. Do not redeploy the old version yet. It may fail against the new schema
   or corrupt data.
2. Open a SEV1 or SEV2 incident in #incidents, depending on user impact.
3. Page the Platform on-call primary and the database owner for your
   service.
4. Decide together whether to roll forward with a fix or to write a
   reverse migration.

- Keep the incident open until the service is stable.
- Revert the faulty commit on `main`, or mark the pull request so the change
  is not released again by accident. The next deployment from `main` would
  otherwise include the same change.
- Write down what you saw and what you did while it is fresh. If the problem
  affected users, the incident needs a blameless postmortem.
- Fix the problem, add a test that would have caught it, and deploy again
  following the deployment runbook.

section_heading: When the pipeline itself is broken
chunk_body:
If the deployment pipeline is unavailable and you must roll back urgently,
page the Platform on-call primary. Platform engineers can roll back a
service directly on the cluster. Do not try to change production resources
by hand yourself, even if you have the access to do so; manual changes are
overwritten by the next deployment and are hard to audit.

**Classification: Confidential. Engineering only.**

This runbook tells engineers what to do when they suspect a security
incident: unauthorised access, leaked credentials, malware, data leaving the
company when it should not, or an attack on a production service. It sits
alongside the On-Call Handbook. Reliability incidents use the SEV levels in
that handbook; security incidents use the SEC levels below, and an event can
have both.

Security Incident Runbook - Introduction

**Classification: Confidential. Engineering only.**

This runbook tells engineers what to do when they suspect a security
incident: unauthorised access, leaked credentials, malware, data leaving the
company when it should not, or an attack on a production service. It sits
alongside the On-Call Handbook. Reliability incidents use the SEV levels in

have both.

chunk_body:
Page the Security Operations on-call through the pager rotation named
**secops-primary**. If there is no acknowledgement within 10 minutes, page
**secops-secondary**, then the Head of Security directly. Do not post
details in #incidents or any public channel. Security Operations opens a
private channel named `#sec-inc-<yyyymmdd>-<codename>` and invites the people
who need to be there.

Codenames are taken in order from the list of Indian rivers kept by Security
Operations, so the incident name never describes the incident.

| Level | Meaning | Response target |
|---|---|---|
| SEC-1 | Confirmed breach of customer or employee personal data, or an attacker active in production | Security lead engaged within 15 minutes, 24x7 |
| SEC-2 | Likely compromise of an internal system or credential with access to production | Within 1 hour, 24x7 |
| SEC-3 | Contained issue with no evidence of data access, such as a leaked test credential | Within 4 business hours |
| SEC-4 | Policy violation or suspicious activity with no clear impact | Next business day |

The Security Operations lead sets the level and may raise or lower it as
facts come in. Any SEC-1 is also treated as a SEV1 for reliability
purposes.

chunk_body:
The goal is to stop the damage without destroying evidence.

1. **Credentials first.** Revoke and rotate any exposed secret straight
   away, following the emergency path in the Key Rotation Runbook. Do not
   wait for confirmation that it was used.
2. **Isolate, do not wipe.** Move affected hosts into the quarantine
   security group `sg-quarantine-forensic`. Never terminate an instance,
   reimage a laptop or delete a container that may be involved.
3. **Snapshot.** Take disk and memory snapshots of affected hosts before
   any change. Snapshots go to the forensic account, which only Security
   Operations can read.
4. **Block.** Add attacker IP ranges and domains to the edge block list.
   Changes to the block list during an incident skip the normal change
   approval.

For a SEC-1, the Head of Security may take any production service offline
without waiting for the CTO. The CTO is informed immediately afterwards.

Legal owns every external notification. Engineers must not contact
customers, regulators or researchers about an incident themselves.

- **CERT-In:** reportable cyber incidents must be reported within 6 hours of
  being noticed. Security Operations prepares the report and Legal files it.
- **Personal data breaches:** Legal - Privacy decides whether the Data
  Protection Board and affected individuals must be told, and prepares the
  notice.
- **Enterprise customers:** most enterprise contracts require notice of a
  confirmed security incident affecting their data within 48 hours of
  confirmation. Legal checks each affected contract.

  new joiners, temporary day badges and visitor passes.

  keys, *Do not use* tags and general questions about the building.
- **IT service desk walk-in counter.** To the right of reception. Collect
  laptops and get help with device problems here.
- **Security office.** Behind reception. This is a restricted area; knock at
  the counter window.
- **Cafeteria.** At the back of the ground floor, serving breakfast and lunch

  cyclists and runners.
- **Wellness room.** Next to the changing rooms. It can be used for rest,
  prayer, nursing or taking medication, and is booked from the calendar like
  a meeting room.

chunk_body:
When you raise a ticket or call the duty line, Facilities gives the problem a
priority.

- **Emergency.** A risk to people's safety or serious damage to the building,
  such as flooding, a gas smell, electrical sparking or a blocked fire exit.
  Someone is sent immediately and the area is made safe first.
- **Urgent.** A problem that stops a floor or team from working, such as no
  power on a floor, no water in the washrooms or a broken main door.
  Facilities aims to respond the same working day.
- **Routine.** Everything else, such as a broken chair, a flickering light or a
  cleaning request. These are scheduled into the maintenance team's work.

If a ticket is not moving, escalate in this order. Always reply on the
original ticket first, so the history stays in one place.

1. **Reply on the ticket.** Explain the impact on your work and ask for an
   update. This alerts the assigned technician and the help desk lead.
2. **Office facilities manager.** Each office has a facilities manager who
   owns the building's day-to-day running. Contact them through the *Office
   contacts* list on the intranet *Workplace* page, and quote the ticket
   number.
3. **Regional workplace lead.** If the office facilities manager cannot
   resolve the issue, or the problem affects more than one office, they will
   escalate to the regional workplace lead. You can also ask your manager to
   contact the regional lead directly.
4. **Head of Workplace Services.** For problems that remain unresolved after
   the steps above, or that involve a serious complaint about a vendor, the
   Head of Workplace Services is the final point of escalation.

Security issues follow a separate path: the Security office, then the office
security manager, then the Head of Corporate Security.

chunk_body:
**Where do I get my ID badge?**
New joiners collect their badge from reception on their first day. Bring a
government photo ID. Your photo is taken at the desk if one was not uploaded
during onboarding.

**What does the badge open?**
The main entrance, the floors your team works on, the pantries and your
locker if it has a badge reader. Restricted areas such as server rooms, the
mail room and the Security office need separate approval.

**How do I get access to another floor or a restricted area?**
Raise a ticket under *Facilities > Access* and name the area and the reason.
Your manager approves the request. Restricted areas also need approval from
the area owner.

**I forgot my badge. Can I still get in?**
Yes. Go to reception with a photo ID. You will get a temporary day badge,
which must be handed in at reception before you leave. Repeatedly forgetting
your badge is reported to your manager.

**I lost my badge. What should I do?**
Report it straight away by calling Security on extension 2222 or raising an
urgent ticket under *Facilities > Access*. Security deactivates the lost badge
and arranges a replacement. A replacement for a lost badge may be charged; the
charge is shown on the ticket.

**My badge stopped working.**
Badges can fail if they are bent or kept next to a phone magnet. Ask reception
to test it. If it is faulty, reception issues a new one.

**Can I let someone in behind me?**
No. Everyone must tap their own badge. Do not hold doors open for people you
do not know, even if they look like employees. Visitors are signed in at
reception under the Visitor Pass Policy.

**Do I have to wear the badge?**
Yes. Wear it visibly on a lanyard or clip at all times in the office.

**What happens when I leave the company?**
Hand in your badge on your last working day as part of exit clearance. It is
deactivated at the end of that day.

This FAQ covers practical questions about getting to the office. Permit
eligibility, charges and car park rules are set by the Office Parking Policy.
Which version of that policy applies to you depends on your office and join
date, so check the policy for the details that apply to you.

**How do I apply for a car parking permit?**
Raise a ticket under *Facilities > Parking* and give your vehicle
registration number. Permits are allocated in the order requests arrive. You
will be told on the ticket when yours is ready to collect.

**How much does a permit cost?**
See the Office Parking Policy. The charge is deducted from salary, and the
amount depends on which version of the policy governs you.

**Can I park a motorcycle or scooter?**
Yes. Two-wheeler parking is in the marked area at the car park entrance. The
Office Parking Policy sets out how it works.

**Is there bicycle parking?**
Yes. Bicycle racks are by the main entrance and are covered by CCTV. Showers
and changing rooms are on the ground floor.

**I have a disability. Can I get a reserved bay?**
Yes. Raise a ticket under *Facilities > Parking* and choose *Accessible bay*.
Your request is kept confidential.

**Can I leave my car overnight?**
Only with approval from Facilities. Ask on a ticket before the day.

**I have changed my car. What do I do?**
Update the registration number on your permit through a Facilities ticket.

**Is there a company shuttle?**
Some offices run a shuttle from the nearest metro station during peak hours.
Timings are posted on the intranet *Workplace* page.

**Where can visitors park?**
Visitor parking is limited. Mention it when you register your visitor under
the Visitor Pass Policy and reception will try to reserve a space.

**Who do I ask about something not covered here?**
The Facilities help desk.

Common questions for the front desk team at every office.

**How do I get a guest into the building?**
Register your visitor in the visitor management system at least 24 hours
before they arrive. The visitor receives a confirmation email, and reception
prints their badge when they check in.

**What does my visitor need to bring?**
A government-issued photo ID. Reception checks it against the registration
before issuing a badge.

**Do I have to meet my visitor at reception?**
Yes. Reception calls you when your visitor arrives, and you must collect them
and escort them at all times while they are in the building.

**Can visitors connect to Wi-Fi?**
Yes, on the guest network. The access code is printed on the visitor badge.

**What happens to the badge when my visitor leaves?**
Walk your visitor back to reception and make sure they hand in the badge.
Badges not returned are deactivated at the end of the day.

**Can I receive a personal delivery at the office?**
Small parcels only. Reception holds them for a few days and emails you when
one arrives.

**Where is lost property kept?**
At reception. Items are kept for one month.

**What are reception's hours?**
Reception is staffed from 8:00 to 20:00 on working days. Outside those hours,
contact the security desk at the main entrance.

chunk_body:
**Do I have a permanent desk?**
No. All offices use shared desks that you book in the workplace app. The How
to Book a Desk guide explains the steps.

**How far in advance can I book a desk?**
The booking window is set by the Desk Booking Policy. The workplace app only
lets you pick dates inside that window.

**What is a neighbourhood?**
An area of a floor set aside for one team so that its members can sit
together. Your manager can tell you which neighbourhood is yours.

**Can I leave my things on the desk overnight?**
No. Desks must be cleared at the end of every day. Use a locker for anything
you want to keep in the office. The End of Day Office Checklist lists what to
do before you leave.

**I need a special chair or a fixed desk for a medical reason.**
Raise a confidential ticket under *Facilities > Workplace adjustments*. The
Desk Booking Policy explains how adjusted and fixed desks work. An occupational
health assessment may be arranged for you.

**What do I do if the fire alarm sounds?**
Leave by the nearest fire exit, do not use the lifts and go to the assembly
point shown on the floor plan. Fire wardens in high-visibility vests will
guide you. Do not go back into the building until a warden tells you it is
safe.

**Where is the first aid kit?**
In every pantry. The names of trained first aiders are posted beside each
kit.

**How do I recycle?**
Use the colour-coded bins in the pantries. Printer toner cartridges and
batteries go to the collection box at the Facilities desk.

**The office is too cold.**
Temperature is set centrally for each zone. If a zone is consistently too hot
or too cold, raise a maintenance ticket rather than adjusting the controls
yourself.

Check with the Facilities desk, where lost property is kept. If you think
something was stolen, report it to Security.

**Can I have a plant or a photo on my desk?**
Not on a shared desk, because it has to be clear at the end of the day. Small
items can be kept in your locker. Teams may put plants in their neighbourhood
with Facilities approval.

Personal electric scooters and e-bike batteries must not be charged indoors
because of the fire risk. Some car parks have charging points; ask the

Workplace and Office Facilities FAQ - Personal items and property

**I lost something in the office.**
Check with the Facilities desk, where lost property is kept. If you think
something was stolen, report it to Security.

**Can I have a plant or a photo on my desk?**
Not on a shared desk, because it has to be clear at the end of the day. Small
items can be kept in your locker. Teams may put plants in their neighbourhood
with Facilities approval.

**Can I charge an electric scooter or vehicle at the office?**
Personal electric scooters and e-bike batteries must not be charged indoors
because of the fire risk. Some car parks have charging points; ask the
Facilities help desk.

chunk_body:

The Facilities help desk, through a ticket or the #ask-facilities channel.
For urgent faults call the duty line on extension 2200, and for emergencies
call Security on extension 2222. The Facilities Escalation Contacts page
explains what to do if a problem is not being fixed.

How to Submit an Expense Claim - Create the claim

1. Open the expense tool from the employee portal.
2. Select *New Claim* and give it a short title, such as *Client visit -
   Chennai - March*.
3. Add one line per expense. For each line:
   - choose the expense category;
   - enter the date shown on the receipt;
   - enter the amount and currency exactly as on the receipt;
   - write the business purpose in one or two sentences;
   - attach the receipt.
4. If you paid in a foreign currency, leave the amount in that currency. The
   tool converts it for you.
5. Check the running total at the top of the claim.
6. Select *Submit*. The claim goes to your line manager.

chunk_body:
Answers to common questions from employees who work with suppliers. For
questions about your own expense claims, see the Expense Claims Policy
instead.

**Where should suppliers send invoices?**
To the Accounts Payable inbox shown on the purchase order. Invoices sent to
you personally are not logged. If one reaches you, forward it to the AP inbox
and tell the supplier to use it next time.

**What must an invoice show?**
The PO number, the company's legal name and GSTIN, the supplier's GSTIN, an
invoice number and date, a description of goods or services that matches the
PO, and the tax broken out by type.

**What happens if there is no PO number?**
AP returns the invoice to the supplier unpaid. The company follows a *no PO,
no pay* rule. If the work was done without a PO, talk to Procurement; a
retrospective PO needs department head approval and is reported to the CFO.

**How does AP decide to pay?**
AP matches three things: the PO, your goods receipt and the invoice. If the
quantity or price differ, the invoice is put on hold and you are notified.

**Why is an invoice on hold?**
The usual reasons are a missing goods receipt, an invoice price above the PO
price, or a quantity greater than you received. The hold reason is shown in
the procurement system. Most holds are cleared by recording the goods receipt
or asking the supplier for a credit note.

**What are the payment terms?**
Standard terms are 45 days from the date AP receives a valid invoice, unless
the contract says otherwise. Payments are released in the weekly supplier
payment run on Thursday.

**Can a supplier be paid early?**
Only with approval from the Finance Controller. Raise a Finance ticket with
the business reason.

**The supplier says they have changed their bank account. What do I do?**
Nothing yourself. Ask them to update the details through the supplier portal.
Procurement verifies every change with a call to a known contact. Treat a
bank change request by email as possible fraud and report it to Finance.

**How do I check whether an invoice has been paid?**
See How to Check a Supplier Invoice's Payment Status.

**Who do I contact?**
Accounts Payable, through a Finance ticket on the employee portal.

chunk_body:
If a supplier asks when they will be paid, you can check the invoice yourself
before contacting Accounts Payable.

1. Open the procurement system from the employee portal.
2. Go to *My Purchase Orders* and open the purchase order.
3. Select the *Invoices* tab. Each invoice shows one of these statuses:
   - *Received* - logged by AP, not yet matched.
   - *On hold* - a mismatch needs your attention; read the hold reason.
   - *Approved* - scheduled for the next supplier payment run.
   - *Paid* - the payment date and reference are shown.

If the invoice is not listed at all, AP has not received it. Ask the supplier
to resend it to the AP inbox with the PO number on it.

chunk_body:
**When is salary paid?**
On the last working day of each month. Payslips are published in the HR
system on the same day.

**What is the payroll cut-off?**
The 20th of each month. Anything that changes your pay has to be approved by
then to be included in that month's salary. Later approvals are processed in
the following month.

**I joined after the cut-off. Will I be paid this month?**
No. Your salary for the days you worked in your joining month is paid with the
next month's salary, together with that month's pay. Your first payslip shows
both amounts as separate lines.

**My salary has not arrived. What should I do?**
First check your payslip in the HR system. If it shows the salary as paid,
the credit may be delayed by your bank; wait until the end of the next
working day. If it still has not arrived, raise an urgent ticket with Payroll
through the HR helpdesk and attach the payslip.

**How do I change the bank account my salary goes to?**
See How to Change Your Salary Bank Account. The change must be approved
before the cut-off to take effect that month.

**Why is my take-home pay different this month?**
Common reasons are an expense reimbursement, a bonus, arrears from a salary

**How is income tax worked out?**
Payroll deducts tax each month based on your expected annual income and the
tax regime you chose. If you do not choose, the default regime set by the
Income Tax Department is used.

**When do I declare my investments?**
In April, in the HR system under *Pay* > *Tax Declaration*. You can update it
during the year; changes approved before the cut-off affect that month's
deduction.

**When do I submit proofs?**
Payroll opens the proof submission window in December and closes it at the
January cut-off. Declarations without proof are removed, and any extra tax is
deducted from the remaining salaries of the financial year.

**When do I get Form 16?**
By 15 June each year, for the previous financial year. It is published in the
HR system under *Pay* > *Tax Documents*.

**I joined mid-year. What do I do about my previous employer's income?**
Upload the Form 12B or payslips from your previous employer in the HR system
so tax is worked out on your full-year income. If you do not, you may owe tax
when you file your return.

for example because they own the software being supported. It must be signed
by the department head. Do not split one purchase into several smaller orders
to stay under a threshold; Finance reviews orders for splitting every quarter.

invoice, and payments are released in the weekly supplier payment run on
Thursday.

chunk_body:

is booked. International travel also needs approval from the department head.
The travel request is raised in the travel portal and must state the purpose of
the trip, the dates, the destination and the estimated cost.

chunk_body:
All flights, trains and hotels must be booked through the company travel portal
or the Travel Desk. Bookings made directly with airlines, hotels or other
websites are not reimbursed unless the Travel Desk has confirmed in writing
that it could not make the booking.
chunk_text:
Business Travel Booking Policy (v1) - Booking channel

All flights, trains and hotels must be booked through the company travel portal
or the Travel Desk. Bookings made directly with airlines, hotels or other
websites are not reimbursed unless the Travel Desk has confirmed in writing
that it could not make the booking.

chunk_body:
Domestic flights must be booked at least **14 days** before the travel
date. International flights should be booked as early as possible once the trip
is approved. Where a trip is arranged at short notice for a genuine business
reason, such as a client escalation, the employee's manager must record the
reason in the travel request; the Travel Desk will then book the best
available fare.

reason in the travel request; the Travel Desk will then book the best
available fare.

chunk_body:
- Domestic flights: economy class for all employees.

- Trains: AC two-tier or equivalent.

own cost or with their own loyalty points.

chunk_body:
Answers to the questions the Travel Desk is asked most often. For anything
not covered here, raise a ticket under *Finance > Travel*.

**How do I book a business trip?**
Submit a travel request in the travel portal with your dates, destination and
cost centre. Once your manager approves it, the Travel Desk books your
tickets and hotel and sends the itinerary to your work email.

**How early do I need to book a domestic flight?**
Domestic flights must be booked at least 14 days before the travel date. If
you cannot meet that, add a short justification to the request and your
manager must approve the late booking.

**Can I book my own tickets and claim them back?**
Only in an emergency, and only with written approval from the Travel Desk.
Keep the booking confirmation and the invoice for your claim.

**Which hotels can I stay in?**
Use the preferred hotels listed in the travel portal. They have negotiated
rates and direct billing, so you do not pay at checkout.

**Can I choose my airline or seat?**
The Travel Desk books the lowest reasonable fare. You can state a preferred
airline in the request, but it is not guaranteed. Seat selection charges are
not covered.

**What if my plans change?**
Tell the Travel Desk as soon as you know, through the same ticket. Changes
made directly with the airline or hotel may not be refunded.

**Do I need travel insurance?**
Company travel insurance covers all approved business trips. The policy
certificate is attached to your itinerary email.

**Who do I call if something goes wrong while travelling?**
The Travel Desk emergency line printed on your itinerary is staffed around
the clock.

chunk_body:
The procurement analyst:
1. Validates the PAN and GSTIN on the government portals and confirms that the
   names match the legal name.
2. Screens the vendor and its directors against the sanctions and debarment
   lists.
3. Checks for conflicts of interest: whether any employee or their close
   relative owns or works for the vendor. The requester must declare any
   known relationship on the request.
4. Confirms MSME status, because MSME suppliers must be paid within the
   period set by law and are flagged in the payment run.
5. Sends the security questionnaire to IT Security where one is required.
   The vendor cannot be approved until IT Security signs it off.

consistently and fairly.
chunk_text:
Background Verification SOP - Purpose

This procedure describes how Talent Acquisition and People Operations run
background verification for new hires, so that every check is done
consistently and fairly.

chunk_body:
It applies to all full-time employees, contract employees and interns hired
by the company.
chunk_text:
Background Verification SOP - Scope

It applies to all full-time employees, contract employees and interns hired
by the company.

chunk_body:
- **Recruiter:** collects the candidate's consent and documents.
- **People Operations:** sends the case to the verification vendor and tracks
  it.
- **Hiring manager:** is informed of the outcome but does not see the detailed
  report.
chunk_text:
Background Verification SOP - Roles

- **Recruiter:** collects the candidate's consent and documents.
- **People Operations:** sends the case to the verification vendor and tracks
  it.
- **Hiring manager:** is informed of the outcome but does not see the detailed
  report.

chunk_body:
1. When the offer is accepted, the recruiter sends the candidate the
   verification consent form through the candidate portal.
2. The candidate uploads identity proof, address proof, education
   certificates and relieving letters from previous employers.
3. The recruiter checks that the documents are complete and legible, then
   hands the case to People Operations.
4. People Operations opens a case with the approved verification vendor. The
   vendor checks identity, address, education, previous employment and, where
   the role requires it, criminal records.
5. People Operations tracks the case in the HR system and follows up with the
   vendor or candidate on any missing information.
6. When the report arrives, People Operations reviews it and marks the case
   *Clear*, *Clear with remarks* or *Discrepancy*.

formal step.

chunk_body:
- **Minor misconduct:** lateness, misuse of company equipment, breaches of
  office rules. Usually handled informally first.
- **Serious misconduct:** repeated minor misconduct, insubordination,
  negligence that causes loss, breaches of the Information Classification
  Standard.
- **Gross misconduct:** theft, fraud, violence, harassment, working under
  the influence of alcohol or drugs, deliberate data leaks. Can lead to
  dismissal for a first offence.

  office rules. Usually handled informally first.

chunk_body:
1. **Initial review.** The manager and Employee Relations decide whether a
   formal process is needed.
2. **Show-cause notice.** The employee receives a written notice setting
   out the allegation and has 72 hours to reply in writing.
3. **Investigation.** An investigating officer at least one grade above the
   employee, and outside their reporting line, gathers evidence. The
   investigation must finish within 20 working days of the notice.
4. **Hearing.** The employee may bring a colleague. The hearing is minuted
   and the minutes are shared with the employee within 3 working days.
5. **Outcome.** The decision is given in writing within 5 working days of
   the hearing.

This procedure explains how employees can raise a workplace concern and how
Employee Relations handles it. It aims to resolve concerns fairly, quickly and
confidentially, and to protect everyone involved from retaliation.
chunk_text:
Grievance Handling SOP - Purpose

This procedure explains how employees can raise a workplace concern and how
Employee Relations handles it. It aims to resolve concerns fairly, quickly and
confidentially, and to protect everyone involved from retaliation.

chunk_body:
The procedure covers concerns about working conditions, treatment by
colleagues or managers, workload, the application of HR policies, and
decisions that affect an employee's employment. It applies to full-time
employees, contract employees and interns.

Complaints of sexual harassment are handled by the Internal Committee under
the Prevention of Sexual Harassment policy, not under this procedure.
Concerns about fraud, bribery or other wrongdoing by the company should be
reported through the whistleblower channel.
chunk_text:
Grievance Handling SOP - Scope

The procedure covers concerns about working conditions, treatment by
colleagues or managers, workload, the application of HR policies, and
decisions that affect an employee's employment. It applies to full-time
employees, contract employees and interns.

Complaints of sexual harassment are handled by the Internal Committee under
the Prevention of Sexual Harassment policy, not under this procedure.
Concerns about fraud, bribery or other wrongdoing by the company should be
reported through the whistleblower channel.

chunk_body:
- **Confidentiality:** information is shared only with people who need it to
  resolve the concern.
- **No retaliation:** raising a concern in good faith never counts against an
  employee. Retaliation is a disciplinary matter.
- **Fairness:** everyone involved has a chance to give their account before a
  decision is made.
- **Right to be accompanied:** the employee may bring a colleague to any
  formal meeting.
chunk_text:
Grievance Handling SOP - Principles

- **Confidentiality:** information is shared only with people who need it to
  resolve the concern.
- **No retaliation:** raising a concern in good faith never counts against an
  employee. Retaliation is a disciplinary matter.
- **Fairness:** everyone involved has a chance to give their account before a
  decision is made.
- **Right to be accompanied:** the employee may bring a colleague to any
  formal meeting.

chunk_body:
Many concerns can be resolved by talking to the person involved or to the
employee's manager. Employees are encouraged to try this first where they feel
comfortable. Managers who receive a concern should listen, take notes, agree
next steps with the employee and follow up. If the concern is about the
manager, the employee may go directly to stage two.
chunk_text:
Grievance Handling SOP - Stage one: informal resolution

Many concerns can be resolved by talking to the person involved or to the
employee's manager. Employees are encouraged to try this first where they feel
comfortable. Managers who receive a concern should listen, take notes, agree
next steps with the employee and follow up. If the concern is about the
manager, the employee may go directly to stage two.

chunk_body:
1. The employee raises a *Confidential* ticket with the HR helpdesk, choosing
   the *Grievance* category, and describes the concern, the people involved
   and the outcome they are looking for.
2. Employee Relations acknowledges the ticket and assigns a case owner who has
   no involvement in the matter.
3. The case owner meets the employee to understand the concern and agrees
   whether an investigation is needed.
4. If an investigation is needed, the case owner or an appointed investigator
   interviews the people involved and reviews relevant documents, such as
   emails, chat records or HR system entries.
5. The case owner prepares a written outcome, setting out the findings, the
   decision and any actions, and meets the employee to explain it.
6. The outcome is recorded in the HR system. Only Employee Relations can see
   the case file.
chunk_text:
Grievance Handling SOP - Stage two: formal grievance

1. The employee raises a *Confidential* ticket with the HR helpdesk, choosing
   the *Grievance* category, and describes the concern, the people involved
   and the outcome they are looking for.
2. Employee Relations acknowledges the ticket and assigns a case owner who has
   no involvement in the matter.
3. The case owner meets the employee to understand the concern and agrees
   whether an investigation is needed.
4. If an investigation is needed, the case owner or an appointed investigator
   interviews the people involved and reviews relevant documents, such as
   emails, chat records or HR system entries.
5. The case owner prepares a written outcome, setting out the findings, the
   decision and any actions, and meets the employee to explain it.
6. The outcome is recorded in the HR system. Only Employee Relations can see
   the case file.

chunk_body:
Where a concern is about how an HR policy has been applied, the case owner
first checks which version of the policy applies to the employee. Several HR
policies, including the Annual Leave Policy, the Work From Home Policy and the
Probation Policy, have more than one version in force, and the applicable
version depends on the employee's join date. Many policy disputes turn out to
be caused by the wrong version being applied; in that case the case owner
arranges for the record to be corrected and closes the grievance.

first checks which version of the policy applies to the employee. Several HR
policies, including the Annual Leave Policy, the Work From Home Policy and the
Probation Policy, have more than one version in force, and the applicable
version depends on the employee's join date. Many policy disputes turn out to
be caused by the wrong version being applied; in that case the case owner
arranges for the record to be corrected and closes the grievance.

is final within the company.

chunk_body:
**Can I work from home?**
Yes. New team members can work from home for up to 3 days per week once they
have completed their first two weeks in the office. The days are agreed with
you and marked in the attendance system by Friday of the previous week.

**Do they need to be in on particular days?**
Yes, on the team's anchor days. Tell them which days those are in the first
week.

This procedure sets out how People Operations, IT, Facilities and the hiring
manager work together to onboard a new employee, from accepted offer to the
end of the first month. Its aim is that every new joiner arrives to a working
laptop, the right access, a desk and a manager who is ready for them.
chunk_text:
New Joiner Onboarding SOP - Purpose

This procedure sets out how People Operations, IT, Facilities and the hiring
manager work together to onboard a new employee, from accepted offer to the
end of the first month. Its aim is that every new joiner arrives to a working
laptop, the right access, a desk and a manager who is ready for them.

chunk_body:
The procedure applies to full-time employees, contract employees and interns
joining any office or joining as remote employees. Internal transfers follow
the Internal Transfer procedure instead.
chunk_text:
New Joiner Onboarding SOP - Scope

The procedure applies to full-time employees, contract employees and interns
joining any office or joining as remote employees. Internal transfers follow
the Internal Transfer procedure instead.

chunk_body:
- **People Operations (onboarding coordinator):** owns the end-to-end process,
  creates the employee record and tracks every step in the onboarding tracker.
- **Talent Acquisition:** hands over the accepted offer and runs background
  verification as described in the Background Verification SOP.
- **Hiring manager:** prepares the team, chooses a buddy and sets objectives.
- **IT End User Services:** prepares the laptop, accounts and access.
- **Facilities:** prepares the ID badge and, where needed, a parking permit.
- **Payroll:** sets up salary payment once bank details are verified.
chunk_text:
New Joiner Onboarding SOP - Roles and responsibilities

- **People Operations (onboarding coordinator):** owns the end-to-end process,
  creates the employee record and tracks every step in the onboarding tracker.
- **Talent Acquisition:** hands over the accepted offer and runs background
  verification as described in the Background Verification SOP.
- **Hiring manager:** prepares the team, chooses a buddy and sets objectives.
- **IT End User Services:** prepares the laptop, accounts and access.
- **Facilities:** prepares the ID badge and, where needed, a parking permit.
- **Payroll:** sets up salary payment once bank details are verified.

chunk_body:
1. Talent Acquisition marks the offer as accepted in the applicant tracking
   system. This automatically creates an onboarding case for People
   Operations.
2. The onboarding coordinator checks the offer details: job title, grade,
   department, location, employment type, manager and date of joining.
3. The coordinator creates a pre-joining record in the HR system. The date of
   joining recorded here is used by the HR system to decide which version of
   each HR policy applies to the employee, so it must match the offer letter
   exactly.
4. The coordinator sends the candidate the pre-joining pack: a welcome note,
   the list of documents to bring, and links to complete personal details
   online.
chunk_text:
New Joiner Onboarding SOP - Stage one: offer accepted

1. Talent Acquisition marks the offer as accepted in the applicant tracking
   system. This automatically creates an onboarding case for People
   Operations.
2. The onboarding coordinator checks the offer details: job title, grade,
   department, location, employment type, manager and date of joining.
3. The coordinator creates a pre-joining record in the HR system. The date of
   joining recorded here is used by the HR system to decide which version of
   each HR policy applies to the employee, so it must match the offer letter
   exactly.
4. The coordinator sends the candidate the pre-joining pack: a welcome note,
   the list of documents to bring, and links to complete personal details
   online.

section_heading: Stage two: before the first day
chunk_body:
1. The coordinator raises the IT onboarding request. IT prepares the laptop
   in line with the Laptop Request and Refresh Policy and creates email,
   chat and HR system accounts.
2. The coordinator asks Facilities to print the ID badge and to arrange a
   parking permit if the joiner has asked for one; the permit terms are in
   the Office Parking Policy.
3. The hiring manager is reminded to complete the tasks in the Manager
   Checklist for New Joiners, including choosing a buddy.
4. The coordinator adds the joiner to the next induction session and sends a
   calendar invitation.
5. The day before joining, the coordinator confirms with IT and Facilities
   that the laptop and badge are ready. Any gap is escalated to the relevant
   team lead the same day.

2. The coordinator asks Facilities to print the ID badge and to arrange a
   parking permit if the joiner has asked for one; the permit terms are in
   the Office Parking Policy.
3. The hiring manager is reminded to complete the tasks in the Manager

4. The coordinator adds the joiner to the next induction session and sends a

5. The day before joining, the coordinator confirms with IT and Facilities

   team lead the same day.

chunk_body:
1. The joiner is greeted at reception, collects their badge and is taken to
   the induction room or joins the induction call.
2. People Operations checks original documents against the copies submitted
   earlier and records the check in the HR system.
3. IT hands over the laptop and helps the joiner sign in, set a password and
   set up VPN access.
4. The joiner completes the First Day Checklist with help from their buddy.
5. The hiring manager meets the joiner and introduces the team.
chunk_text:
New Joiner Onboarding SOP - Stage three: first day

1. The joiner is greeted at reception, collects their badge and is taken to
   the induction room or joins the induction call.
2. People Operations checks original documents against the copies submitted
   earlier and records the check in the HR system.
3. IT hands over the laptop and helps the joiner sign in, set a password and
   set up VPN access.
4. The joiner completes the First Day Checklist with help from their buddy.
5. The hiring manager meets the joiner and introduces the team.

chunk_body:
1. The joiner attends the company induction, which covers company history,
   values, the Code of Conduct, information security and how to find HR
   policies.
2. The joiner completes mandatory e-learning modules in the learning portal.
   The coordinator monitors completion and reminds joiners who fall behind.
3. The hiring manager agrees probation objectives with the joiner and records
   them in the HR system, following the timing in the Probation Policy.
4. Payroll confirms that bank details have been verified before the first
   salary run.
5. At the end of the first month, the coordinator sends a short onboarding
   survey and closes the onboarding case.

4. Payroll confirms that bank details have been verified before the first
   salary run.
5. At the end of the first month, the coordinator sends a short onboarding
   survey and closes the onboarding case.

During induction, People Operations explains that several HR policies,
including the Annual Leave Policy, the Work From Home Policy and the
Probation Policy, have more than one version in force at the same time, and
that the version that applies depends on the employee's date of joining.
Joiners are shown how to read the applicability section of a policy. The
induction deliberately does not quote allowances, deadlines or durations from
those policies, to avoid giving out figures from the wrong version.

chunk_body:

is a guide, not a forced curve, but any group that is more than 5 points

chunk_body:
A calibration group is a department, or a part of a department, with at
least 15 rated employees. Smaller teams are pooled with a related team so
that the distribution means something. Each group is chaired by the
department head, with the HR Business Partner as facilitator. A session is
valid only if at least two thirds of the managers in the group attend.

chunk_body:
1. A rating of 5 needs at least two concrete examples of impact beyond the
   employee's own team, and must be supported by a second manager in the
   room.
2. A rating of 1 is allowed only if the employee was told in writing about
   the performance gap at least 90 days before the end of the review year.
   If that did not happen, the lowest rating the committee can give is 2.
3. A rating of 2 or 1 for two cycles in a row triggers a performance
   improvement plan, run with the HR Business Partner.
4. Managers may not calibrate their own ratings upward after the session.
   Any change after calibration needs the department head and the HR
   Business Partner to sign off.

This guide explains how the annual performance review works and what
employees and managers need to do at each step. It covers confirmed
employees. Reviews for employees still on probation follow the Probation
Policy instead.
chunk_text:
Performance Review Guide - Introduction

This guide explains how the annual performance review works and what
employees and managers need to do at each step. It covers confirmed
employees. Reviews for employees still on probation follow the Probation
Policy instead.

chunk_body:
Reviews give every employee a clear, fair picture of how they are doing,
recognise good work and agree where to grow next. They also feed into
decisions on pay increases and promotions, so they need to be done carefully
and on time.
chunk_text:
Performance Review Guide - Why we review performance

Reviews give every employee a clear, fair picture of how they are doing,
recognise good work and agree where to grow next. They also feed into
decisions on pay increases and promotions, so they need to be done carefully
and on time.

chunk_body:
1. **Goal setting** at the start of the year.
2. **Mid-year check-in** to review progress and adjust goals.
3. **Year-end review**, made up of a self-review, peer feedback and a manager
   review.
4. **Calibration** across teams.
5. **Review conversation** and sharing of the final rating.

People Operations announces the dates for each step on the employee portal.

Performance Review Guide - The cycle at a glance

1. **Goal setting** at the start of the year.
2. **Mid-year check-in** to review progress and adjust goals.
3. **Year-end review**, made up of a self-review, peer feedback and a manager
   review.

5. **Review conversation** and sharing of the final rating.

chunk_body:
Employees draft goals in the HR system under *Performance* > *Goals*. Good
goals are specific, measurable and linked to the team's objectives. Most
employees have a small number of goals, each with a short description of
what success looks like. Managers review the draft, discuss it with the
employee and approve it. Goals can be changed during the year if priorities
change; record the change in the HR system so that the review reflects it.
chunk_text:
Performance Review Guide - Step one: set goals

Employees draft goals in the HR system under *Performance* > *Goals*. Good
goals are specific, measurable and linked to the team's objectives. Most
employees have a small number of goals, each with a short description of
what success looks like. Managers review the draft, discuss it with the
employee and approve it. Goals can be changed during the year if priorities
change; record the change in the HR system so that the review reflects it.

chunk_body:
The mid-year check-in is a conversation, not a rating. The employee and
manager discuss progress against each goal, what support is needed and any
goals that should be updated. The manager records a short summary in the HR
system.
chunk_text:
Performance Review Guide - Step two: mid-year check-in

The mid-year check-in is a conversation, not a rating. The employee and
manager discuss progress against each goal, what support is needed and any
goals that should be updated. The manager records a short summary in the HR
system.

chunk_body:
Employees write a self-review against each goal. Give concrete examples of
what you delivered and how, and be honest about what did not go well and what
you learned. Link to documents or dashboards where that helps.
chunk_text:
Performance Review Guide - Step three: year-end review > Self-review

Employees write a self-review against each goal. Give concrete examples of
what you delivered and how, and be honest about what did not go well and what
you learned. Link to documents or dashboards where that helps.

section_heading: Step three: year-end review > Peer feedback
chunk_body:
Employees nominate colleagues who have worked closely with them to give
feedback. Managers may add or replace reviewers. Feedback should be specific,
balanced and focused on behaviour and outcomes, not personality. Peer
feedback is shared with the employee without the reviewer's name.
chunk_text:
Performance Review Guide - Step three: year-end review > Peer feedback

Employees nominate colleagues who have worked closely with them to give
feedback. Managers may add or replace reviewers. Feedback should be specific,
balanced and focused on behaviour and outcomes, not personality. Peer
feedback is shared with the employee without the reviewer's name.

section_heading: Step three: year-end review > Manager review
chunk_body:
The manager reads the self-review and peer feedback, then writes an overall
assessment and proposes a rating. The rating scale and its descriptions are
shown in the HR system next to the rating field.
chunk_text:
Performance Review Guide - Step three: year-end review > Manager review

The manager reads the self-review and peer feedback, then writes an overall
assessment and proposes a rating. The rating scale and its descriptions are
shown in the HR system next to the rating field.

chunk_body:
Managers in each department meet to compare proposed ratings, so that similar
performance receives similar ratings across teams. Managers should come
prepared with evidence for each rating. Ratings may change during
calibration; the manager explains any change to the employee.

Performance Review Guide - Step four: calibration

Managers in each department meet to compare proposed ratings, so that similar

chunk_body:
The manager and employee meet to discuss the review. The manager shares the
final rating, explains the reasons and agrees development goals for the next
year. The employee then acknowledges the review in the HR system and can add
comments. Acknowledging a review does not mean agreeing with it.
chunk_text:
Performance Review Guide - Step five: review conversation

The manager and employee meet to discuss the review. The manager shares the
final rating, explains the reasons and agrees development goals for the next
year. The employee then acknowledges the review in the HR system and can add
comments. Acknowledging a review does not mean agreeing with it.

chunk_body:
- Keep a simple record of achievements through the year so that the
  self-review is easy to write.
- Ask for feedback regularly rather than waiting for the year-end review.
- If you disagree with your rating, first talk to your manager. If that does
  not resolve it, you may raise it through the Grievance Handling SOP.

Performance Review Guide - Tips for employees

- Keep a simple record of achievements through the year so that the

- Ask for feedback regularly rather than waiting for the year-end review.

chunk_body:
- Hold regular one-to-ones throughout the year so that nothing in the review
  is a surprise.
- Base ratings on evidence and outcomes, not on where or when the work was
  done. Employees working from home under the Work From Home Policy are
  assessed in the same way as those in the office.
- Watch for common biases, such as giving more weight to recent events or
  rating people like yourself more favourably.
- Do not discuss other employees' ratings.

This policy describes the probation period for new employees and how it is
reviewed and confirmed.
chunk_text:
Probation Policy (v1) - Purpose

This policy describes the probation period for new employees and how it is
reviewed and confirmed.

chunk_body:
Every new employee serves a probation period of **6 months** starting on
their date of joining. During probation the employee and manager agree clear
objectives in the first two weeks and hold a documented check-in at the
midpoint of the probation period.
chunk_text:

chunk_body:
At the end of probation the manager completes a confirmation review in the HR
system. The outcome is one of: confirmed, extended, or not confirmed. HR sends
a confirmation letter to the employee once the review is approved.
chunk_text:

chunk_body:
Probation may be extended once, for a period agreed between the manager and
HR, where there is a clear performance or conduct concern that the employee has
a fair chance to address. The reasons must be recorded in writing and shared
with the employee.

chunk_text:

chunk_body:
- Up to 10 roles: department head and the Chief People Officer.
- 11 to 50 roles: the Chief People Officer and the Chief Financial Officer.
- More than 50 roles, or any closure of an office: the Board.
chunk_text:
Redundancy Process - Approvals

- Up to 10 roles: department head and the Chief People Officer.
- 11 to 50 roles: the Chief People Officer and the Chief Financial Officer.
- More than 50 roles, or any closure of an office: the Board.

chunk_body:
Where only some roles in a pool are affected, employees are scored on a
selection matrix: skills needed for the future structure (40 percent),
performance ratings from the last two cycles (35 percent), and
disciplinary record (25 percent). Length of service is used only as a tie
break. Employees on maternity leave, on long medical leave or who have
raised a grievance in the last twelve months cannot be selected without a
review by Legal.

find an internal role during consultation move without a trial period.

chunk_body:
The company pays more than the statutory minimum:

- **Severance pay:** 30 days of basic pay for every completed year of
  service, with a floor of 90 days of basic pay and a cap of 24 months of
  basic pay.
- **Notice pay:** paid in lieu of the full contractual notice.
- **Medical cover:** group medical cover for the employee and dependants
  continues for 180 days after the exit date.
- **Outplacement:** a career transition service for 120 days, including CV
  support and interview coaching.
- **Leave:** all unused earned leave is encashed, whatever the normal cap.

The package is paid only after the employee signs a separation agreement,
which Legal drafts. Employees are given 10 working days to review it.

This policy rewards employees who refer candidates that the company goes on to

chunk_body:
A successful referral earns a bonus of **INR 50,000** per hire, paid to the
referring employee. The amount is the same for all roles and levels.
chunk_text:

chunk_body:
- The referral must be submitted through the referral portal before the
  candidate applies through any other channel.
- The referred candidate must not have applied to the company in the
  preceding six months.
- Hiring managers, recruiters and HR business partners are not eligible for a
  bonus on roles they are directly hiring for.
- Referrals of former employees are eligible only if they left the company
  more than twelve months earlier.

chunk_body:
The company uses nine grades. G1 to G5 are individual contributor grades.
G6 is the first manager grade, and "manager grade and above" in any
restricted document means G6 to G9.

| Grade | Title | Track |
|---|---|---|
| G1 | Associate | Individual contributor |
| G2 | Senior Associate | Individual contributor |
| G3 | Specialist | Individual contributor |
| G4 | Senior Specialist | Individual contributor |
| G5 | Principal | Individual contributor |
| G6 | Manager | Management |
| G7 | Senior Manager | Management |
| G8 | Director | Management |
| G9 | Vice President | Management |

A G5 Principal who moves into people management is re-graded to G6 only if
the role has at least four direct reports. Otherwise the employee stays at
G5 with the Principal title.

chunk_body:
Compa-ratio is an employee's fixed pay divided by the midpoint of their
band. It is the main measure Total Rewards uses to judge whether someone is
paid fairly for their grade.

| Compa-ratio | Position | What it usually means |
|---|---|---|
| Below 0.85 | Low in band | New to grade, or underpaid |
| 0.85 to 1.05 | In range | Fully competent in the role |
| 1.05 to 1.20 | High in band | Long-serving or consistently strong |
| Above 1.20 | Above band | Red-circled; see below |

chunk_body:
- New hires are offered between the band minimum and the midpoint. An offer
  above the midpoint needs written approval from the HR Business Partner and
  the department head. An offer above a compa-ratio of 1.10 also needs the
  Chief People Officer.
- An offer may never exceed the band maximum. If a candidate's expectation
  is above the maximum, Talent Acquisition must check whether the role has
  been graded correctly before going back to the candidate.
- Joining bonuses are capped at 20 percent of annual fixed pay and are
  clawed back in full if the employee leaves within twelve months of
  joining.

model: collaboration happens best in the office, while focused work can often
be done from home.
chunk_text:
Work From Home Policy (v1) - Purpose

This policy sets out when employees may work from home, how to arrange it and
what is expected of them while working remotely. The company operates a hybrid
model: collaboration happens best in the office, while focused work can often
be done from home.

chunk_body:
This policy covers full-time employees, contract employees and interns alike.
Contractors and interns follow the same rule as full-time employees; for them,
the join date is the start date of their current contract or internship.
chunk_text:
Work From Home Policy (v1) - Scope

This policy covers full-time employees, contract employees and interns alike.
Contractors and interns follow the same rule as full-time employees; for them,
the join date is the start date of their current contract or internship.

chunk_body:
Eligible employees may work from home for up to **3 days** per week.
Unused days do not carry over to the following week and cannot be combined
into a longer block of remote working.
chunk_text:
Work From Home Policy (v1) - Allowance

Eligible employees may work from home for up to **3 days** per week.
Unused days do not carry over to the following week and cannot be combined
into a longer block of remote working.

chunk_body:
Each team agrees one or two anchor days per week on which everyone is expected
in the office. Work-from-home days should not be taken on a team's anchor days
unless the manager agrees in advance.
chunk_text:
Work From Home Policy (v1) - Anchor days

Each team agrees one or two anchor days per week on which everyone is expected
in the office. Work-from-home days should not be taken on a team's anchor days
unless the manager agrees in advance.

section_heading: How to arrange work from home
chunk_body:
1. Mark the days in the attendance system by Friday of the previous week.
2. Tell your manager if you plan to change a day at short notice.
3. Keep your calendar status set to "Working remotely" on those days.

Managers may decline or reschedule a work-from-home day where the business
need requires the employee on site, for example for a client visit, an
audit or an incident review.

chunk_body:
Employees working from home keep the same core hours as in the office, 10:00
to 16:00 local time, and must be reachable on chat and phone during those
hours. Meetings should be joined with the camera on where practical.

connection. Company laptops must be used for all work; personal devices may not

Working from home does not change what is expected of an employee. Managers
assess performance on outcomes, not on where the work is done. Teams should

This matrix explains how IT problems are prioritised, who works on them at
each stage and when a ticket is escalated. It is for all employees, and
especially for managers and team leads who need to know when to push a problem
further. It covers incidents (something is broken) rather than requests

This matrix explains how IT problems are prioritised, who works on them at
each stage and when a ticket is escalated. It is for all employees, and
especially for managers and team leads who need to know when to push a problem
