chunk_body:
Every incident is given a priority when it is logged. The service desk sets the
priority from two things: how many people are affected and how badly their
work is stopped.

| Priority | Description | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| P1 - Critical | A core service is down for a whole office, department or the company, or there is an active security incident. | Email down for everyone; office network outage; ransomware alert; confirmed account compromise. |
| P2 - High | A core service is down for a team, or one person cannot work at all and there is no workaround. | A team cannot reach the finance system; a laptop will not start on the day of a client presentation. |
| P3 - Medium | One person's work is disrupted but a workaround exists. | A printer queue is stuck; one application crashes but the web version works. |
| P4 - Low | A minor issue, question or cosmetic problem. | A display setting; a request for advice on an application feature. |

If you believe the priority on your ticket is wrong, reply on the ticket and
explain the business impact. The service desk will review it. Do not raise a
second ticket for the same problem.

chunk_body:
**Tier 1 - IT service desk.** Receives every ticket, call and chat. Resolves
account unlocks, multi-factor resets, application questions, basic device
faults and anything covered by a published how-to guide. Tier 1 logs the
incident, sets the priority and either resolves it or passes it to Tier 2.

**Tier 2 - Specialist teams.** End User Services handles laptop hardware,
device management and the software catalogue. Identity and Access handles
accounts, groups, single sign-on and privileged access. Network Security
handles the VPN, office Wi-Fi and firewalls. Collaboration Services handles
email, calendar, chat and meeting rooms.

**Tier 3 - Platform engineers and vendors.** Senior engineers who own a
platform, and external vendors under support contracts. Tier 3 is engaged by
Tier 2, never directly by employees.

Security incidents always start at P1, whatever their apparent size, until IT
Security has assessed them. They include:

- a lost or stolen laptop, phone or security key,
- a multi-factor prompt that you approved but did not start,
- an email you clicked on and then realised was phishing,
- signs that someone else has used your account.

Report these by phone to the IT service desk, not by ticket or chat, so that
the desk can act straight away. The desk will bring in IT Security. Do not try
to investigate or clean up the problem yourself, and do not turn off an
affected laptop unless IT Security asks you to.

section_heading: When and how to escalate yourself
chunk_body:
Most tickets do not need escalating; the service desk tracks them against the
targets above. Escalate yourself only if:

- the impact has become worse since you raised the ticket,
- a deadline makes the problem more urgent than it first looked, or
- the ticket has had no update for longer than the table allows.

To escalate, reply on the ticket with the word **ESCALATE** in the first line
and explain the reason. This notifies the service desk team lead. If you get
no response within half a working day, your manager can contact the IT
Operations Manager directly, quoting the ticket number.

Plain-English definitions of IT terms you will see in company guides and
tickets. Where a term is governed by a policy, the policy is named so you can
check the current rules there.

**Asset tag.** The sticker with a barcode on every company device. Quote it in
tickets about hardware.

**Device management.** The service that installs security settings and
software on company laptops and phones, and can lock or wipe them if they are
lost.

**Gateway.** A VPN server you connect to. The VPN client picks the nearest one
when set to *Automatic*.

**Idle timeout.** The period of inactivity after which a session is ended
automatically. For the VPN, the value is set in the VPN Access Policy.

**IT service portal.** The website where you raise tickets and requests for
IT, and track their progress.

**Loaner laptop.** A temporary laptop issued while your own is being repaired
or has not yet arrived.

**Multi-factor authentication (MFA).** Signing in with something you know
(your password) and something you have (an approval on your phone).

**Passphrase.** A password made of several unrelated words. The rules that
passwords must meet are in the Password Rules policy.

**Phishing.** An email or message that pretends to be from someone trusted in
order to steal your credentials or install malware.

**Refresh cycle.** How often a laptop is replaced with a new model. The cycle
is set in the Laptop Request and Refresh Policy and differs between groups of
employees.

**Security key.** A small USB device used as a second factor for highly
privileged accounts.

**Self-service software catalogue.** The app on company laptops for
installing approved software without a ticket.

**Single sign-on (SSO).** Signing in once with your company account to reach
many applications.

**Split tunnelling.** Sending some traffic through the VPN and some directly
to the internet. Whether it is used is set in the VPN Access Policy.

**Ticket.** A record of a request or problem in the IT service portal. Each
ticket has a reference number.

metadata.title: How to Raise a HelpLine Ticket

chunk_body:
1. Open HelpLine from the *Quick Links* box on the intranet home page, or
   go to `http://helpline.corp.local`.
2. Log in with your Windows username and password.
3. Click *Log a Call*.
4. Choose a category: *Hardware*, *Software*, *Network*, *Access* or
   *Admin*.
5. Write a one-line summary and a description of the problem. Include your
   desktop's computer name from the asset sticker.
6. Click *Submit*. You get an email with your call number, starting *HL-*.

This policy explains how employees in the Engineering department get a

chunk_body:
Every new employee receives a company laptop on their first day. The hiring
manager raises the laptop request in the IT service portal when the offer is
accepted, choosing from the standard models below. If the request is raised
late, IT provides a loaner laptop until the standard device arrives.

manager raises the laptop request in the IT service portal when the offer is
accepted, choosing from the standard models below. If the request is raised
late, IT provides a loaner laptop until the standard device arrives.

chunk_body:
- **Standard profile:** 14-inch Windows laptop, 16 GB RAM, 512 GB SSD.
- **Developer profile:** 16-inch laptop, 32 GB RAM, 1 TB SSD, available as
  Windows or macOS.

The profile is set by the employee's role. A different profile needs approval
from the department head and a written business justification.

chunk_body:
Laptops are replaced on a **4-year** refresh cycle, counted from the date
the device was first issued. IT contacts the employee about two months before
the refresh date to schedule the swap. Employees cannot request an early
refresh simply because a newer model is available.
chunk_text:

the device was first issued. IT contacts the employee about two months before
the refresh date to schedule the swap. Employees cannot request an early
refresh simply because a newer model is available.

chunk_body:
A laptop is replaced before its refresh date only if:
- it has a hardware fault that IT cannot repair economically,
- it has been lost or stolen and a report has been filed with IT Security, or

Transcript of a knowledge transfer session for new End User Services team
members on handling equipment from employees who are leaving. Lightly edited.

**Presenter:** When HR confirms a resignation, a leaver ticket is created
automatically and lands in our queue. It lists every asset registered to the
person: laptop, monitors, headset, phone, security key.

**Attendee:** Do we contact the leaver straight away?

**Presenter:** Yes. Send the *Leaver equipment* email template the same day.
It tells them what they need to hand back and where.

**Attendee:** And the deadline?

**Presenter:** Everything has to be returned within 7 working days of their
last working day. Office-based people usually drop things at the IT desk on
their last day. Remote people get a prepaid courier box.

**Attendee:** What if something is missing when it comes back?

**Presenter:** Record it on the ticket and tell HR. Missing items are
recovered from the final settlement, so HR needs to know before payroll
closes the person's account.

**Attendee:** Do we wipe the laptop right away?

**Presenter:** No. Hold it for thirty days in case the manager needs data
recovered. After that, wipe it, check its condition and put it back into
stock or send it for disposal.

**Attendee:** What about their accounts?

**Presenter:** Identity and Access disable those on the last working day. We
only handle the hardware.

**Presenter:** Questions? Otherwise that is leavers done.

metadata.title: Working Remotely with the Remote Desktop Gateway

chunk_body:
1. Your manager approves remote access in a HelpLine ticket.
2. IT issues you an RSA hardware token. Collect it from the IT room on the
   4th floor and sign the token register.
3. Leave your office desktop switched on and logged out. Do not shut it down
   when you leave, or you will not be able to reach it.
chunk_text:

1. Your manager approves remote access in a HelpLine ticket.
2. IT issues you an RSA hardware token. Collect it from the IT room on the
   4th floor and sign the token register.
3. Leave your office desktop switched on and logged out. Do not shut it down
   when you leave, or you will not be able to reach it.

metadata.title: Working Remotely with the Remote Desktop Gateway

chunk_body:
1. On your home computer, open *Remote Desktop Connection*.
2. Click *Show Options* and enter your desktop's computer name. It is on the
   asset sticker on the front of the PC, for example `BLR-DT-0217`.
3. On the *Advanced* tab, click *Settings* and enter the gateway address
   `rdgw.corp.local`.
4. Click *Connect*. When asked, enter your Windows username and password,
   followed by the six-digit code shown on your RSA token.

section_heading: Keeping data safe away from the office
chunk_body:
- **Lock your screen** every time you step away, even at home.
- **Keep your laptop with you** when travelling. Never leave it in a car, even
  in the boot, and never check it in as hold luggage.
- **Watch who can see your screen** on trains, planes and in cafes. A privacy
  screen filter can be requested through the IT service portal.
- **Keep calls private.** Do not discuss confidential matters where you can be
  overheard.
- **Do not print confidential documents at home.** If you must print, use an
  office printer.
- **Store files in company storage**, not on the laptop's desktop or in
  personal cloud accounts. Files in company storage are backed up; files on
  the laptop are not.
- **Family and friends** must not use your company laptop, even briefly.

Passwords and multi-factor authentication work the same way at home as in the
office. The requirements are in the Password Rules policy, and the company
password manager is the only approved place to store work passwords.

A short set of answers to the security questions new joiners ask in their
first week.

**What are the rules for my account password?**
Your password must be at least 12 characters long and must not contain your
name or username. A passphrase of several unrelated words is easier to
remember than a random string and just as strong.

**Can I reuse a password I use somewhere else?**
No. Your work password must be unique. Never use it for personal accounts or
other websites.

**Where should I store my passwords?**
In the company password manager. Do not write passwords down or keep them in
a document or spreadsheet.

**Why do I have to approve sign-ins on my phone?**
Multi-factor authentication stops someone who has guessed or stolen your
password from signing in. Only approve a prompt if you started the sign-in
yourself.

**I think I clicked a phishing link. What now?**
Report it straight away with the *Report phishing* button in your mail client
and raise a ticket with the Service Desk. Reporting early is never a problem.

**Can I use a USB stick to move files?**
No. Use approved cloud storage to share files. USB storage is blocked on
company laptops.

**Should I lock my laptop when I step away?**
Always. Press Windows+L on Windows or Ctrl+Cmd+Q on a Mac. Screens lock
automatically after a short period, but do not rely on that.

**Who do I ask about something not covered here?**
The IT Service Desk.

chunk_body:
Transcript of a knowledge transfer session recorded for new Service Desk
analysts. Lightly edited for readability.

**Presenter:** Today we are going through software requests, because they are
about a fifth of our tickets. First thing: always check whether the software
is already in the self-service catalogue. If it is, point the user there and
close the ticket. They do not need approval for catalogue items.

**Attendee:** And if it is not in the catalogue?

**Presenter:** Then it has to come in as a software request on the service
portal. Make sure the request has the software name, the version, the
business reason and whether a paid licence is needed. If any of that is
missing, send it back to the user before it goes to their manager.

**Attendee:** Who approves it?

**Presenter:** The user's manager. If IT Security has never assessed the
software, it also goes to them for review. You will see the *Security
review* flag on the ticket.

**Attendee:** What do we tell users about timing? That is what they always
ask.

**Presenter:** Once it is approved, we install it or add it to the
catalogue within 5 business days. If a new paid licence is needed and
procurement gets involved, it can take longer, and the user is given an
expected date when the request is approved.

**Attendee:** What if someone asks for something on the prohibited list?

**Presenter:** Reject it and quote the policy. Peer-to-peer tools, cracked
software, personal VPNs and unapproved remote-access tools are never
allowed, however senior the person asking is.

**Attendee:** Browser extensions?

**Presenter:** Same rules as any other software. Only extensions on the
approved list.

**Presenter:** That is it for software. Next session covers access requests.

repaired.

This policy describes how employees connect to company systems from outside
the office using the virtual private network (VPN), and the security controls
that apply to VPN sessions.
chunk_text:
VPN Access Policy (v1) - Purpose

This policy describes how employees connect to company systems from outside
the office using the virtual private network (VPN), and the security controls
that apply to VPN sessions.

chunk_body:
The VPN is required to reach internal systems such as the intranet, internal
code repositories, finance systems and the HR system when working from outside
a company office. Cloud applications that use single sign-on, such as email and
chat, do not need the VPN.
chunk_text:
VPN Access Policy (v1) - Who needs the VPN

The VPN is required to reach internal systems such as the intranet, internal
code repositories, finance systems and the HR system when working from outside
a company office. Cloud applications that use single sign-on, such as email and
chat, do not need the VPN.

chunk_body:
VPN access is enabled automatically for all employees when their account is
created. The VPN client is pre-installed on company laptops. Access from
personal devices is not permitted.
chunk_text:
VPN Access Policy (v1) - Getting access

VPN access is enabled automatically for all employees when their account is
created. The VPN client is pre-installed on company laptops. Access from
personal devices is not permitted.

chunk_body:
1. Open the VPN client from the system tray or menu bar.
2. Select the nearest gateway, or leave the client on "Automatic".
3. Sign in with your company credentials.
4. Approve the multi-factor authentication prompt on your phone.
chunk_text:
VPN Access Policy (v1) - Connecting

1. Open the VPN client from the system tray or menu bar.
2. Select the nearest gateway, or leave the client on "Automatic".
3. Sign in with your company credentials.
4. Approve the multi-factor authentication prompt on your phone.

chunk_body:
- A VPN session that has no network activity for **60 minutes** is
  disconnected automatically and the employee must sign in again.
- Every session, active or not, is ended after 12 hours and requires a fresh
  sign-in with multi-factor authentication.
- Only one VPN session per user may be open at any time. Signing in on a
  second device ends the first session.

This page answers common questions about problems with the VPN client. The
rules for VPN use, including how long a session can stay open, are in the

section_heading: The VPN client says "Unable to reach gateway". What should I do?
chunk_body:
Check that you can open a public website. If you can, switch the client to a
different gateway or to *Automatic*. Hotel and airport networks sometimes block
VPN traffic; try a mobile hotspot instead.
chunk_text:
VPN Troubleshooting FAQ - The VPN client says "Unable to reach gateway". What should I do?

Check that you can open a public website. If you can, switch the client to a
different gateway or to *Automatic*. Hotel and airport networks sometimes block
VPN traffic; try a mobile hotspot instead.

section_heading: I was disconnected without doing anything. Is something wrong?
chunk_body:
Probably not. Sessions end automatically after a period of inactivity, and
after a maximum duration, as described in the VPN Access Policy. Sign in again
to reconnect.
chunk_text:
VPN Troubleshooting FAQ - I was disconnected without doing anything. Is something wrong?

Probably not. Sessions end automatically after a period of inactivity, and
after a maximum duration, as described in the VPN Access Policy. Sign in again
to reconnect.

section_heading: My VPN keeps dropping when I sign in on another device.
chunk_body:
The VPN Access Policy limits how many sessions you can have open at once, so
signing in on a second device can end the first. Disconnect on the device you
are not using.
chunk_text:

The VPN Access Policy limits how many sessions you can have open at once, so
signing in on a second device can end the first. Disconnect on the device you
are not using.

chunk_body:
Declare a conflict as soon as you notice it, even if you are not sure it
counts.

1. Open the Legal portal and choose **Declare a conflict of interest**.
2. Select the type: outside job, family relationship, financial interest,
   gift or other.
3. Describe the situation in plain words and name the people or companies
   involved.
4. Add your manager as the reviewer.
5. Submit the form.

Your manager and the Compliance team review the declaration and record an
agreed action. Until you hear back, step back from any decision that the
conflict could affect.

to do about it. It applies to all employees, contractors and interns. For
the declaration form itself, see How to Declare a Conflict of Interest.

section_heading: What a conflict of interest is
chunk_body:
A conflict of interest arises when your personal interests, or those of
people close to you, could influence, or look as if they influence, the
decisions you make for the company. Having a conflict is not wrong in
itself. Hiding one is.

The test is simple: if a colleague, customer or journalist learned about the
situation, would they reasonably question whether you acted in the
company's best interest? If the answer might be yes, declare it.

section_heading: What to do when you spot a conflict
chunk_body:
1. **Declare it.** Use the form in the Legal portal. Declare as soon as you
   become aware of the conflict, not when a decision is due.
2. **Step back.** Until the declaration is reviewed, do not take part in
   decisions that the conflict could affect. Tell the people you work with
   that you have stepped back, without needing to give details.
3. **Follow the agreed action.** Your manager and Compliance will record one
   of the following:
   - *No action needed.* The conflict is noted and you carry on.
   - *Managed.* You carry on with safeguards, such as a second approver on
     decisions involving the other party.
   - *Removed.* Someone else takes over the relationship or decision.
   - *Not permitted.* You must end the outside activity or interest.
4. **Update it.** If your situation changes, submit a new declaration. The
   annual compliance certification also asks you to confirm that your
   declarations are up to date.

Answers to common questions about signing documents electronically. For the
steps to send a document, see How to Send a Document for E-Signature.

**Is an electronic signature legally valid?**
Yes, for most commercial agreements. A few document types still need a wet
ink signature or stamp paper, such as some property documents and powers of
attorney. Legal will tell you when a document needs this.

**Who can sign on behalf of the company?**
Only the authorised signatories listed in the Delegation of Authority
matrix. Signing a contract you are not authorised to sign can make you
personally responsible for it, so do not sign even if the other party asks
you to.

**Can I use a scanned image of my signature instead?**
No. A pasted image does not record who signed or when. Always use the
e-signature tool, which keeps an audit trail.

**The other party wants to use their own e-signature tool. Is that allowed?**
Usually yes. Forward the signing email to Legal Operations first so they can
check the document matches the approved version.

**A signer has not signed. What should I do?**
Use **Remind** in the envelope. If the signer has left the other
organisation, void the envelope and send a new one to the right person.

**I spotted a mistake after sending. Can I edit the envelope?**
No. Void the envelope, fix the document, get it re-approved by Legal if the
change is more than a typo, and send a new envelope.

**Where do I find a signed copy later?**
Search the contract repository by the other party's name or the contract
request number.

chunk_body:
Answers to common questions about the intellectual property (IP) clause in
your employment contract.

**What did I agree to when I signed my contract?**
Your contract assigns to the company the IP in anything you create in the
course of your job. This covers code, designs, documents, inventions and
data. You keep the right to be named as the author or inventor where the law
gives you that right.

**Does this cover things I make in my own time?**
Not usually. Work you do outside working hours, without company equipment or
confidential information, and that is not related to our business, stays
yours. If a side project is close to what the company does, declare it
before you start so there is no dispute later.

**How do I declare a side project?**
Use the conflict-of-interest declaration form in the Legal portal and choose
**other**. Describe the project and how it differs from your work here.
Legal replies in writing, and you should keep that reply.

**What about things I created before I joined?**
They stay yours. If you want to use any of them in your work here, list them
with Legal first. Otherwise it may be hard to show later that they existed
before you joined.

**Can I contribute to open-source projects?**
Yes, within the Open Source Contribution Guidelines published by
Engineering. Contributions made as part of your job need approval from your
engineering manager. Personal contributions to projects unrelated to our
products do not.

**Can I publish a paper or give a conference talk about my work?**
Yes, after review. Send the draft to Legal and your manager before you
submit it, so that we can check it does not reveal confidential information
or an invention we plan to patent.

**What happens if I invent something patentable?**
Tell your manager and submit an invention disclosure in the Legal portal.
Do not discuss it outside the company until Legal has decided whether to
file a patent. Inventors named on a filed patent receive a recognition award
under the Inventor Recognition Programme.

**Does the assignment continue after I leave?**
The assignment of work you created while employed does not end when you
leave. You must also keep confidential information confidential after you
leave.

**Who can I ask?**
Raise a question in the Legal portal under **IP and inventions**.

chunk_body:
You need a signed NDA before you share confidential information with anyone
outside the group. Confidential information includes product roadmaps,
source code, pricing, customer lists, unreleased financial results and
anything marked "Internal" or "Confidential".

You do not need an NDA to:

- share information that is already public, such as our website or press
  releases;
- talk to a supplier about their standard products and published prices;
- speak to a recruiter about a role, as long as you share only the job
  description.

If you are unsure, treat the information as confidential and ask Legal.

Quick answers about keeping and deleting company records. The periods for
each type of record are in the Records Retention Schedule.

**What is a record?**
Any information created or received in the course of business that shows
what the company did or decided. Contracts, board minutes, approved budgets
and signed forms are records. Drafts, duplicates and chat about lunch are
not.

**Where should records be kept?**
In the system of record for that type: the contract repository for
contracts, the HR system for employee files, the finance system for
accounting documents. Personal drives and inboxes are not systems of record.

**Why can't I just keep everything?**
Keeping data longer than needed breaks data protection law, costs money to
store and makes searches during a dispute slower and riskier.

**Can I delete a record early?**
No. Records must be kept for the full period in the schedule, even if they
seem no longer useful.

**What is a legal hold?**
An instruction from Legal to keep certain records because of a dispute,
investigation or audit. A legal hold overrides the schedule: do not delete
anything covered by it, even if its period has ended. You will receive an
email naming the hold, and you must confirm it.

**What happens to my files when I leave?**
Your manager reviews your drive before your account is closed and moves any
records into the right system. Anything left is deleted with the account.

**Who do I ask about a record that is not in the schedule?**
Raise a question in the Legal portal under **Records and retention**.

  If there is none, the record is deleted.

approved it. Do not list the personal data itself in the log.
